title: The Engraver of Bukhara: the Silent Remembrance, the Teachers Out of Order, and the Village Renamed
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Village and the Third Day

stops.name: Qasr-i Hinduvan, the birth
stops.date_confidence: contested. Wikipedia and ghayb.com give 14 Muharram 718 AH, March 1318; the order's own Golden Chain page gives Muharram 717 AH, 1317. Neither acknowledges the other; day and month are not recoverable, so the date defaults to 01-01.
stops.campa: In a village ten kilometers from Bukhara, in the month of Muharram, a son is born to a Persian-speaking Tajik household of the oasis. The place is called Qasr-i Hinduvan, the Palace of the Indians. Seventy-one years later it will be renamed for the child. The earliest texts do not explain how he comes by the name Naqshband, the engraver; the order that will carry that name supplies the reading afterward, taking naqsh for the imprint of God's name pressed into a heart. Bukhara at this hour is a hundred years past its sack and still counting.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Kasri Orifon', for the village's modern coordinates and its 10 km distance from Bukhara

stops.name: Qasr-i Hinduvan, the third day
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The three-days-after-birth encounter is transmitted by the order's own literature and by Wikipedia as tradition; no independent chronicle records it.
stops.campa: Three days after the birth the wandering Khwajagan master Muhammad Baba as-Samasi passes through the village. He takes the infant up, blesses him, and adopts him as a spiritual son. What he says over the child is transmitted in one sentence about engraving, and the whole later history of the order folds into it: a name given before the boy can hear it, a tariqa named for a mark not yet made. Samasi stands in the line of Yusuf Hamadani and of Abd al-Khaliq al-Ghujdawani, who has been dead a hundred and forty years.
stops.quote: Allah's name is going to be engraved (Naqsh) on his heart. And the Order will take its name from this engraving.
stops.quote_source: naqshbandi.org, 'Muhammad Baba as-Samasi', as the order transmits the words spoken over the infant
suggested_refs: naqshbandi.org, 'Muhammad Baba as-Samasi', for the wording of the declaration

stops.name: Bukhara, the grandfather's instruction
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources. The order records the grandfather's role and the boy's routine without any year; 1325 is placed here only to hold the episode in sequence.
stops.campa: It is his grandfather, not his parents, who brings him to live near the city. The old man sets him a rule that the boy will keep and later describe in his own voice: rise long before the dawn prayer and spend the dark in supplication. In Bukhara the walls stand, the markets work, and the scholars have come back; Genghis Khan burned this city a century ago and Ibn Battuta, passing through in ruin twelve years ago, found the madrasas empty and the learned scattered. The boy is raised in what grew back.
stops.quote: I would arise early, three hours before Fajr prayer
stops.quote_source: naqshbandi.org, 'The Naqshbandi Golden Chain', where the passage is given as instruction received from his grandfather
suggested_refs: naqshbandi.org's Golden Chain page, which attributes this routine to the grandfather and not to any shaykh

stops.name: Samas, service to Baba Sammasi at eighteen
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and in open conflict with TDV. naqshbandi.org puts him in Samas serving Sammasi at eighteen; TDV states Sammasi died before Naqshband reached adulthood, which cannot be squared with a service beginning c. 1336. Not adjudicated. Village coordinates approximate: naqshbandi.org places Samas in the suburbs of Ramitan, northwest of Bukhara.
stops.campa: At eighteen he is sent to the village of Samas to serve the master who blessed him as an infant. The bond declared over a three-day-old child is now a discipline with hours in it: attendance, errands, silence, the slow transfer of a method that is not written down. Samas sits in the suburbs of Ramitan, northwest of Bukhara across the Zarafshan, a day's walk from the village where he was born. He arrives as a spiritual son already named and stays as a servant.
suggested_refs: naqshbandi.org, 'Muhammad Baba as-Samasi', locating Samas near Ramitan

stops.name: Samarqand, the dream of Khalil Ata
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed backward from TDV's twelve years ending in 748/1347. The location is unsupported: no source names the seat of Khalil Ata's court, and TDV says only that it lay in Chagatai Khanate territory. Samarqand stands here as the region's capital, not as an attested site.
stops.campa: He sees a face in a dream and then finds it, waking, in the person of a Turkic shaykh of the Yasawi line who has become a ruler in the Chagatai country. Naqshband enters his service and stays. The atlas already knows this road: baha_ud_din_walad's household passed through Samarqand in 1212 with the five-year-old Rumi, in a Transoxiana that still had its walls, its libraries, its markets, and did not yet know what was coming down out of the east. Naqshband comes to the same city as a servant of the men who came after.
suggested_refs: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Bahaeddin Naksibend', on the Chagatai service and its end in 748/1347

stops.name: Konye-Urgench, the amir's affairs in Khwarazm
stops.date_confidence: hagiographic and undated. No source dates or independently attests this leg; it belongs to the devotional account of the court period and the year is a placeholder within it.
stops.campa: The service carries him north and west to Khwarazm, to the old capital on the Amu Darya delta that Genghis Khan's armies broke a century and a quarter earlier. Ibn Battuta, riding the same country in 1333, will name Bukhara and Khwarazm in one breath as the two poles of the cold he remembers. Naqshband is here on a ruler's business, not a shaykh's, and the sources that carry him here carry no date, no errand, and no incident. He is a man in his twenties or thirties riding a dead empire's roads for a living master, and the order will later have to explain this decade away.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Konye-Urgench, capital of Khwarazm before the Mongol destruction

stops.name: Samarqand, the fall of Khalil Ata
stops.date_confidence: attested by TDV as 748/1347, the one firm date in this phase. The duration is contradictory: naqshbandi.org gives six years with Khalil Ata, TDV gives twelve. Twelve years ending in 1347 collides with the service under Sammasi said to begin c. 1336. Both readings stand; neither is adjusted.
stops.campa: In 748 the ruler falls and the court dissolves. Naqshband walks out of political life and does not enter it again. The order's own telling gives him six years here; the Turkish encyclopedia gives him twelve and ends them precisely, in the year the Chagatai power that fed him breaks. Between the two accounts sits an unresolved decade, and inside that decade also sits his service to Sammasi. The sources do not sequence the two. They simply both happened.
suggested_refs: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Bahaeddin Naksibend', for the 748/1347 terminus and the twelve-year figure

stops.name: Romitan, the death of Baba Sammasi
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Naqshbandi sources place Sammasi's death in the mid-1350s, commonly 755/1354; TDV's claim that he died before Naqshband's adulthood contradicts this and is not reconciled.
stops.campa: The master who blessed him three days after his birth dies in the Ramitan country. Sammasi has already named his successor, and the succession does not pass to the man he adopted as a son: it passes to Sayyid Amir Kulal, a potter's son. Naqshband is in his middle thirties, has served two masters, has come out of a fallen court with nothing, and now attaches himself to a third. The engraving declared over his cradle has taken thirty-six years and has not yet produced an order.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Muhammad Baba as-Samasi in the Ramitan district of the Bukhara oasis

stops.name: Vabkent, the madrasa of Amir Kulal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the relationship and for Kulal's madrasa at Vabkent; the start year is inferred from Sammasi's death. The 'roughly twelve years with Amir Kulal' of earlier summaries is unsupported: TDV says only many years, and the twelve-year figure belongs to Khalil Ata.
stops.campa: North of Bukhara, at Vabkent, Sayyid Amir Kulal heads a madrasa. He is a potter's son and a wrestler by reputation, and he becomes Naqshband's principal teacher for the rest of his life. The instruction here is not textual. It is a way of holding the breath against a formula, and it is given hand to hand. Kulal will name no successor in the chain but this man, and the order that carries Naqshband's name will run its descent back through this provincial madrasa and its clay.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Amir Kulal', on his headship of the madrasa at Vabkent

stops.name: Vabkent, negation and affirmation
stops.date_confidence: undated. Naqshband's own account of the instruction survives without a year; 1356 holds it in sequence within the Kulal decades.
stops.campa: Kulal teaches him nafy va ithbat, negation and affirmation: the first half of the testimony held on an out-breath, the second driven into the heart, the whole thing counted and timed and never spoken aloud. The silent dhikr is passed to him in private, apart from the circle. What is transmitted here is not a doctrine but a technique, and the technique is what the order will still be doing six hundred years later in rooms from Anatolia to Kashgar.
stops.quote: Our way is companionship, and all goodness is in gathering with the righteous.
stops.quote_source: As rendered by Aal-e-Qutub, aalequtub.com, citing Rashahat 'Ayn al-Hayat; the Rashahat provenance is uncorroborated and returns no match in Open Library full-text search
suggested_refs: Rashahat 'Ayn al-Hayat of Fakhr al-Din 'Ali Safi, the order's foundational memoir collection, not accessed directly in this pass
sources: ghayb.com, quoting Naqshband's own account of Kulal's instruction

stops.name: Ghijduvan, the master a hundred and forty years dead
stops.date_confidence: undated, and the location is doctrinal rather than biographical. The uwaysi bond is a visionary relationship; no source records a physical visit to Ghijduvan. The town holds the pin because the grave is there.
stops.campa: Abd al-Khaliq al-Ghujdawani lies at Ghijduvan, dead since 1179. Naqshband takes him as a master anyway. The order calls this uwaysi, discipleship without a living teacher, transmission across a hundred and forty years of ground. Ghujdawani had laid down eight principles and had already insisted on remembrance kept purely silent; the practice had lapsed. Naqshband does not invent the silence. He revives it, and receives from a grave the authority to say so.
stops.quote: The aim in dhikr is that the heart be always aware of al-Haqq, for its practice banishes inattention.
stops.quote_source: J. Spencer Trimingham, The Sufi Orders in Islam (Oxford), glossing Yad kard, one of the eight principles of 'Abd al-Khaliq al-Ghujdawani and not among the three Naqshband is credited with adding
suggested_refs: The mausoleum of 'Abd al-Khaliq al-Ghujdawani at Gijduvon
J. Spencer Trimingham, The Sufi Orders in Islam, on the eleven principles
sources: J. Spencer Trimingham, The Sufi Orders in Islam

stops.name: Sokhar, the burial of Amir Kulal
stops.date_confidence: attested as 770/1370 for the death; village coordinates approximate and the tomb site not independently pinpointed in this pass.
stops.campa: Amir Kulal dies at Sokhar near Ramitan and is buried there. Naqshband is past fifty and has now outlived every teacher who ever laid a hand on him. Nothing bearing his name yet exists. The men who will carry the order are not yet gathered, the eleven principles are not yet counted, and the only thing he has that no one can take is a method for keeping the heart occupied without moving the tongue. He goes back to the villages and works the ground, and the order dates nothing at all in the two decades that follow.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Sayyid Amir Kulal at Sokhar, near Ramitan in the Bukhara oasis

stops.name: Nasaf, Qutham Shaykh and Arif Dikgarani
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The two teachers are attested by name; no source consulted places Naqshband personally at Nasaf, and TDV grants Dikgarani only a brief association, not the seven years earlier summaries gave him.
stops.campa: South of Bukhara, at the old town of Nasaf that the maps now call Qarshi, sit two more masters of the Khwajagan line: Mawlana Kuthum Shaykh, whom he follows for years, and Mawlana Arif ad-Dikgarani, with whom the Turkish encyclopedia allows him only a brief association. Both names survive. Neither is attached to a place he is recorded reaching or a year he is recorded arriving. The teachers of this life are a list, not a sequence, and the list does not agree with itself about how long any of them held him.
suggested_refs: naqshbandi.org, 'Arif ar-Riwakri', the thirteenth-century figure with whom Dikgarani has been repeatedly conflated

stops.name: Deqqaron, the village that keeps the teacher's name
stops.date_confidence: hagiographic and undated. Coordinates are an approximate placement in the Bukhara oasis; the modern site was not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: A village in the oasis carries the teacher's name in Naqshbandi memory, and tradition puts Naqshband there serving and studying for a further stretch of years. The order remembers this the way it remembers most of the middle of his life: as a duration without a boundary, a place without a road to it. He is by now a man in his fifties attaching himself to teachers, which is not what a founder is supposed to be doing. The name Naqshband already exists. Nothing is attached to it yet, and no one in the oasis is waiting for anything.
suggested_refs: Naqshbandi hagiographic tradition naming 'Arif Deqqarani among Naqshband's masters
sources: Naqshbandi hagiographic tradition, relayed through modern biographical summaries

stops.name: Nurata, the desert and the hands at work
stops.date_confidence: hagiographic and undated; the retreat years are a framing in the devotional literature rather than a dated episode.
stops.campa: He takes to the steppe margins east of Bukhara, to the Nurata country, for solitary retreat and manual labor. The motto the order will hang on him afterward belongs to these years whether or not he ever said it: the hands stay at the work, the heart stays with the Friend. It is an argument as much as a slogan. Against the ecstatic Sufism of the ruined-tavern school it proposes a mystic who is indistinguishable, from outside, from a farmhand. The order will repeat the phrase for six centuries without anyone locating it in a text he wrote.
stops.quote: Dil ba yar o dast ba kar
stops.quote_source: The order's motto, universally attributed to Baha al-Din Naqshband but untraceable in this pass to the Rashahat, the Anis al-Talibin, or the Maqamat-i Bahauddin; encountered only in informal secondary mentions
suggested_refs: The Nurata range and its springs, edge of the steppe east of the Bukhara oasis
sources: Naqshbandi hagiographic tradition summarizing the post-training retreat years

stops.name: Ramitan, working the land
stops.date_confidence: hagiographic and undated. Note that the 'hidden years' framing of earlier summaries collapses: Kulal did not die until 1370, so any period of obscurity begins after that, not in 1354.
stops.campa: Tradition names Ramitan among the villages where he works the ground in the quiet years before the teaching becomes public. It is the same district that holds Samas, where he served Sammasi as a young man, and Sokhar, where Kulal is buried. His whole world at this point is a ring of villages around one city, perhaps forty kilometers across. Everything the order will later claim about his travels has to be fitted around this fact and mostly is not.
suggested_refs: The Ramitan district of the Bukhara oasis, holding both Samas and Sokhar

stops.name: Chaharjuy, the Amu Darya crossing
stops.date_confidence: route inference, the thinnest tier. TDV attests three journeys out of Bukhara but names no waypoints; no source places Naqshband at this crossing.
stops.campa: The Turkish encyclopedia records three journeys away from Bukhara, two of them pilgrimages. It records no roads. Anyone leaving the oasis for Khorasan crosses the Amu Darya near Chaharjuy, where the river runs wide and slow and the ferrymen work the same bank they worked for Marco Polo's father and uncle, who spent three years trading in Bukhara from 1264 and learned, in their own account, the Tartar tongue and manners. The crossing is inferred. The journeys are not.
suggested_refs: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Bahaeddin Naksibend', on the three journeys and two hajj trips
sources: Route inference from medieval Transoxiana-Khorasan caravan geography

stops.name: Merv, the oasis on the Khorasan road
stops.date_confidence: route inference. No dated episode is attached to Merv in any source consulted; the stop marks the road, not an event.
stops.campa: Merv sits between Bukhara and the Iranian plateau, the great oasis on the Khorasan road, a city Genghis Khan's armies emptied in 1221 and that has never come back to what it was. The hagiographic itineraries run Naqshband through it because everyone ran through it. There is no episode here, no teaching, no meeting. There is a route and a man who is known to have travelled three times, and the two are laid over each other in the absence of anything better.
suggested_refs: The ruin fields of Merv on the Bukhara-to-Khorasan road
sources: Route inference from standard 14th-century caravan roads

stops.name: Sarakhs, the frontier waystation
stops.date_confidence: route inference, flagged as weak reconstruction. No source names Naqshband at Sarakhs.
stops.campa: Sarakhs marks the line between Khorasan and Transoxiana, a caravan stop with wells and a customs post and nothing recorded of Naqshband in it. It is included the way a waystation is included: to keep the road honest, so the distance between Bukhara and Mecca is not folded into a single line on a map. The journeys the sources credit him with are months of walking, and this is what the months look like: wells, tolls, dust, and a border that means nothing to a pilgrim and everything to a tax collector. The hagiographies skip it. The road does not.
suggested_refs: The caravanserai and frontier post at Sarakhs on the Khorasan road
sources: Route inference from medieval Bukhara-Khorasan caravan geography; no source names Naqshband here

stops.name: Nishapur, the road Attar walked
stops.date_confidence: route inference. Some tellings route him through Nishapur toward Mecca; none attaches a dated incident. The coordinate is the atlas's existing Nishapur pin, shared with attar and rumi.
stops.campa: Nishapur is the Khorasani center of Sufi learning on the westward pilgrim road, and the atlas already stands in it twice. Here attar blessed the child rumi and put the Asrar-nama in his hands, predicting he would set fire to the hearts of the world's lovers; here the Mongols killed attar in the sack eight years later. Naqshband comes through, if he comes through, a century and a half after that, on a road whose greatest names are already dead and already legends.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Attar at Nishapur, on the westward road out of Transoxiana
sources: Route inference from medieval hajj roads out of Central Asia

stops.name: Bastam, the tomb of Bayazid
stops.date_confidence: doctrinal, not biographical. Naqshbandi tradition credits Bistami with a secondary uwaysi transmission into the order; no source places Naqshband physically at Bastam. Flagged as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Abu Yazid al-Bistami has lain at Bastam for five hundred years, and Naqshbandi tradition runs a second uwaysi thread back to him, transmission again from a grave. The atlas holds this tomb twice already: abu_yazid_al_bistami as his own journey, and attar kneeling here to gather sayings for the Tadhkirat al-Awliya. Bistami is the man who said glory be to me, how great is my station. The order Naqshband gives his name to will be built partly to make such sentences unnecessary.
suggested_refs: The shrine complex of Bayazid Bistami at Bastam

stops.name: Herat, the Khorasani shaykh
stops.date_confidence: attested by TDV, which records the Herat visit and the meeting with a Khorasani shaykh; the year within the journeys is not given. Earlier summaries treated a Persian Wikipedia silence on Herat as a contradiction; that is an argument from omission and is withdrawn.
stops.campa: At Herat, under Kartid rule and about to be pulled into Timur's orbit, he meets a shaykh of Khorasan. This is the one stop outside the Bukhara oasis that a rigorous reference work positively attests. The Turkish encyclopedia names the man as Zeynuddin el-Hafi, who died in 1435 and cannot be him; the figure intended is almost certainly Zayn al-Din Abu Bakr Taybadi, who dies the same year Naqshband does. Even the attested stop arrives with the wrong name attached.
suggested_refs: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Bahaeddin Naksibend', the only consulted source positively attesting the Herat visit

stops.name: Taybad, the shaykh's own town
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the location is contradicted. Earlier summaries sent Naqshband to Taybad to sit with Zayn al-Din Abu Bakr Taybadi; TDV puts the encounter at Herat instead. The Taybad stop is retained as tradition only.
stops.campa: Zayn al-Din Abu Bakr Taybadi keeps his khanaqah at Taybad, southeast of Herat toward the desert. Tradition sends Naqshband here to sit with him; the better source keeps the meeting at Herat and sends nobody to Taybad. Both stops stand in this journey because the discipline of the atlas is to leave the two roads on the map rather than pick one and pretend the other was never told. The shaykh here dies in 1389, the same year Naqshband does, which is the kind of coincidence that makes a tradition want a meeting whether or not there was one.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Zayn al-Din Abu Bakr Taybadi at Taybad, Khorasan
sources: Modern biographical summaries naming Taybadi among Naqshband's teachers

stops.name: Balkh, the disputed southern circuit
stops.date_confidence: disputed and possibly a conflation with other Khwajagan masters who did travel the southern road. Found in popular accounts only; absent from every core biographical summary consulted.
stops.campa: A minority strand puts him on the southern circuit through Balkh, the mother of cities. The atlas has been here: baha_ud_din_walad's household is documented in this province by a waqf document before it fled west, and out of that flight came Rumi. Naqshband's presence has no such document and probably no basis. It is included as what it is, a claim in circulation that the sources will not carry, and it is not resolved. Other Khwajagan masters did ride this road, and the likeliest explanation is that one of their itineraries was quietly handed to him by a later copyist.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia and the Iranica corpus on Balkh under Kartid and early Timurid rule
sources: Minority devotional tradition; not found in Wikipedia summaries accessed

stops.name: Baghdad, the tomb of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani
stops.date_confidence: the weakest-attested stop in the set. Later Naqshbandi devotional telling places him at the shrine; no core biographical summary carries it, and it reads as retrospective lineage-building. The coordinate is the atlas's existing shrine pin from abdelkader.journey.json.
stops.campa: In the Bab al-Sheikh quarter of eastern Rusafa lies abd_al_qadir_al_jilani, and some later Naqshbandi tellings bring Naqshband to the tomb, binding the Khwajagan chain to the Qadiri one at a single grave. The atlas has watched this happen before: in 1826 abdelkader, an eighteen-year-old Algerian pilgrim named for the saint, knelt at this exact stone and renewed his father's chain. Naqshband's kneeling here is not attested. The impulse behind the story is the same impulse.
suggested_refs: The mausoleum of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani at Bab al-Sheikh, Baghdad
sources: Later Naqshbandi devotional tradition; not found in core biographical summaries

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba
stops.date_confidence: attested. TDV records three journeys out of Bukhara including two hajj trips; the years are not given. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Kaaba pin, already shared by nine other journeys.
stops.campa: He makes the hajj twice. The Turkish encyclopedia states it plainly, which settles a question the devotional literature could only assert and the shorter modern summaries were silent on. The man who spends his life arguing that remembrance should be inaudible, unwitnessed, and indistinguishable from ordinary labor circles the House twice among a hundred thousand people doing the loudest and most visible thing in Islam. He is in his late fifties or older.
suggested_refs: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Bahaeddin Naksibend', on the two hajj journeys

stops.name: Medina, the Prophet's Mosque
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Hagiographic accounts pair the hajj with a visit to the Prophet's tomb; TDV attests the pilgrimages without naming Medina. The coordinate is the atlas's existing Prophet's Mosque pin.
stops.campa: Pilgrims coming from Mecca go north to the green dome, and the accounts pair the two as a matter of course. What Naqshbandi tradition wants from Medina is larger than a visit: the order holds that he received instruction directly from the Prophet, in vision, without a living intermediary. Two of his three masters are dead men. The chain he stands in is built as much out of graves as out of teachers, and the order says so without embarrassment. A living master can be contradicted. A dead one, reached in vision, transmits without argument, and the transmission cannot be audited by anyone.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque and the Rawda at Medina

stops.name: Bukhara, Khwaja Bala-gardan
stops.date_confidence: attested for the epithet and the patronage; undated, and the year is placed in his last decade to hold sequence.
stops.campa: The city gives him a name of its own. Khwaja Bala-gardan, the master who turns calamity aside, and after that, patron saint of Bukhara. His following is urban and Tajik-speaking, tradesmen and scholars of the oasis, and it does not look like a movement. There is no lodge, no rule written down, no dues. There is a man in a city who is understood to be holding something off, and a method that leaves no sound in the room where it is practiced. Bukhara has been sacked, rebuilt, sacked again, and traded through by four empires. It knows what it wants from a saint, and what it wants is protection.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Baha-ud-Din Naqshband Bukhari', on the epithet Khwaja Bala-gardan

stops.name: Po-i-Kalyan, the minaret Genghis leaves standing
stops.date_confidence: inferred continuity of place, not an attested episode. No sermon or dated event of Naqshband's is recorded at the Friday mosque; the minaret's survival and the atlas's other visits to it are attested.
stops.campa: The great minaret stands at the center of the city, spared in 1220 when genghis_khan burned everything around it and told Bukhara from the Friday mosque that he was the punishment of God. ibn_battuta saw it standing over rubble in 1333. Naqshband knows it as the ordinary landmark of his ordinary walk. Five centuries after him gurdjieff will come to this same complex hunting what he calls the reservoir of the dervishes, looking for lineages older than the mosques, and find the tariqa this man's silence started.
suggested_refs: The Po-i-Kalyan complex and the Kalyan minaret of 1127

stops.name: Bukhara, three principles added to eight
stops.date_confidence: tradition, undated. The order credits Naqshband with the three additions; Trimingham's account confirms the eleven-principle structure without dating the addition.
stops.campa: Ghujdawani had left eight principles. Naqshband is credited with three more: awareness of the moment, the counting of recitations, the heart held to a single point. Eleven in all, and the whole apparatus of the order is in them. The rule is not to feel more. The rule is to keep the count, watch the clock, and not lose the thread while the market is loud. He rejects the music and the dancing that other orders keep. Nothing about his practice can be seen from outside a room.
stops.quote: We prefer silent dhikr because it preserves the dignity of the Shari'ah and avoids ostentation.
stops.quote_source: As rendered by Aal-e-Qutub, aalequtub.com, citing Rashahat 'Ayn al-Hayat; the wording was verified on that page but the Rashahat provenance returns no match in Open Library full-text search
suggested_refs: J. Spencer Trimingham, The Sufi Orders in Islam, on the eleven Naqshbandi principles
sources: J. Spencer Trimingham, The Sufi Orders in Islam

stops.name: Bukhara, the sober rule
stops.date_confidence: attested for the teaching; undated.
stops.campa: The teaching is narrow and it is meant to be. Hold to the Sunnah. Keep the law. No sama, no ecstatic utterance, no station claimed aloud. Two centuries earlier rumi had staged the question at Konya, when Shams asked which was greater, the Prophet who confessed he had not known God as God deserved, or Bistami who said glory be to me. Naqshband's whole order is an answer to that question, delivered not as argument but as procedure, and it will grow larger than any other in Islam.
suggested_refs: islam.wiki, 'Baha' ad-Din an-Naqshbandi', on the rejection of sama

stops.name: Bukhara, Muhammad Parsa and Ala al-Din Attar
stops.date_confidence: attested for both successors; the year is placed in his last decade and is not given by the sources.
stops.campa: In the last years the men who will carry it gather. Sayyid Ala al-Din al-Bukhari al-Attar receives what the order calls the secret; Khwaja Muhammad Parsa is named alongside him as a transmitter of the teaching. Neither is asked to build an institution. At least one account holds that the tariqa becomes an institution only after his death, and that sixty years on there are still only a scattering of small communities across Mawarannahr and Khurasan. The engraving spreads slowly.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Baha-ud-Din Naqshband Bukhari', naming Ala al-Din al-Attar as successor

stops.name: Chaganiyan, the successor's country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; a regional placement associated with Ala al-Din Attar, not with Naqshband, who is not recorded travelling there. Coordinates approximate.
stops.campa: Ala al-Din Attar is tied by tradition to the Chaganiyan country southeast of Bukhara, up the Surkhan valley toward the mountains. Naqshband himself is not recorded going there. The point is the reach: before the founder is dead the order already has a second address, a day or two of hard riding from the first, in country that answers to different amirs. It is not yet a network. It is two towns and the road between them, and within a century it will be the largest order in Islam, running from the Balkans to Kashgar on a discipline that fits inside one man's chest.
suggested_refs: The Surkhan valley and the medieval region of Chaganiyan
sources: Naqshbandi lineage tradition regarding Ala al-Din Attar's regional base

stops.name: Qasr-i Arifan, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested and now resolved. Wikipedia and ghayb.com give 2 March 1389; naqshbandi.org gives Monday night, 3 Rabi' al-Awwal 791, converting it wrongly to 1388. The Hijri year is consistent across all sources. TDV confirms 3 Rabi' al-Awwal 791 = 2 March 1389, resolving the second-or-third ambiguity to the third. Age about 71 solar, 73 lunar.
stops.campa: He dies on a Monday night in his native village and is buried in his own garden. The village is renamed for him: Qasr-i Hinduvan becomes Qasr-i Arifan, the Palace of the Gnostics, and the maps carry the new name still, ten kilometers from Bukhara. He is seventy-one solar years old, seventy-three by the moon. He leaves a method, two successors, no institution, and a corpus of writings that a Turkish encyclopedia will later go through and mostly return.
stops.quote: Monday night, the 3rd of Rabi'ul-Awwal, 791 H.
stops.quote_source: naqshbandi.org, 'The Naqshbandi Golden Chain', which converts this date to 1388; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi converts the same Hijri date to 2 March 1389
suggested_refs: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi, 'Bahaeddin Naksibend', converting 3 Rabi' al-Awwal 791 to 2 March 1389

stops.name: Qasr-i Arifan, the khanqah of the Shaybanid
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1544-1545. Earlier summaries described this as a tomb built over the grave; Wikipedia states it is the khanqah, the largest building of the complex. The grave structure predates it.
stops.campa: A hundred and fifty-five years after the burial, the Shaybanid Khan Abd al-Aziz raises a khanqah over the site, the largest building in what is becoming a complex. It is not a tomb built over a grave. The grave was already marked; this is expansion, the moment a saint's garden turns into architecture with a budget. By now the order carries his name from Anatolia to India, and the shrine has to be the size of what has grown out of it. The man who refused music, dancing, and any practice a bystander could witness is given the largest building in the Bukhara oasis outside the city walls.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Bahoutdin Architectural Complex', on the 1544-1545 khanqah

stops.name: Bahoutdin, the minaret and its dated inscription
stops.date_confidence: attested; the year is recorded in a Nasta'liq inscription on the minaret itself.
stops.campa: The minaret goes up under the emirate of Bukhara, its year written into the brick in Nasta'liq so that no one afterward has to guess. Around it now: mosques, the Shaybanid khanqah, a madrasah, courtyards, and at the center the dahma, the gravestone, fenced in carved marble latticework. The man buried under it taught that the practice should leave no trace an onlooker could see. Thirteen years later gurdjieff will walk into this country looking for exactly that trace.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Bahoutdin Architectural Complex', on the 1885 minaret and its inscription

stops.name: Bahoutdin, the grave closed
stops.date_confidence: attested that visiting was forbidden under Soviet rule; no source consulted gives the year the prohibition began, so the date is a placeholder within the Soviet period.
stops.campa: Under Soviet rule visiting the grave is forbidden. The shrine stands, the brick stands, and the practice goes where it has always been able to go, which is inside a person, counted, timed, and inaudible. Of all the Sufi orders to be banned in Central Asia, this is the one whose central discipline requires no building, no music, no gathering, and no sound. The prohibition holds for most of a century and the order does not die. Whatever the state closes, it closes a building; the eleven principles were designed in the fourteenth century to survive exactly this and were never written for a room.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Bahoutdin Architectural Complex', on the Soviet prohibition

stops.name: Kasri Orifon, the asphalt road
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1951 by Wikipedia, 'Kasri Orifon'.
stops.campa: In 1951, with pilgrimage to the grave officially forbidden, an asphalt road is built from Bukhara to the shrine. The state that has closed the site paves the way to it. Ten kilometers, two or three hours on foot in the fourteenth century, now a short drive. The village that gave him his first name and took his second keeps both: Qasr-i Hinduvan on the old maps, Kasri Orifon on the new ones, the Palace of the Gnostics in the plural. Nobody in 1951 is admitting that the road is for pilgrims. Everybody driving it knows.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Kasri Orifon', on the 1951 road from Bukhara to the shrine

stops.name: Bahoutdin, the 675th anniversary
stops.date_confidence: attested. Note that a 675th anniversary in 1993 counts from 1318, adopting the Wikipedia and ghayb.com birth year against naqshbandi.org's 1317.
stops.campa: Two years into Uzbek independence the shrine is rebuilt for the six hundred and seventy-fifth anniversary of his birth. The arithmetic is a decision: 1993 minus 675 is 1318, which quietly picks one of the two contested birth years and puts it in stone. In 2003 the calligrapher Habibulloh Solih writes Quranic inscriptions across the gate. A Sufi museum and a research center open in 2004, a plaque goes up in 2009, and the restoration continues into 2010.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Bahoutdin Architectural Complex', on the 1993, 2003, 2004, 2009 and 2010 works

stops.name: Bahoutdin, the Zarafshan-Karakum corridor
stops.date_confidence: attested. Tentative List 18 January 2008; transnational inscription 2023, month and day not given for the latter.
stops.campa: Uzbekistan puts the complex on the UNESCO Tentative List in January 2008, and in 2023 it is written into the transnational inscription for the Silk Roads: Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor. The village where a wandering shaykh blessed a three-day-old child is now a listed segment of a trade route, held jointly by three states. Pilgrims come to the dahma in its marble cage, and the practice the man taught still cannot be photographed, because it was designed from the start to make no sound.
suggested_refs: UNESCO, 'Silk Roads: Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor', inscribed 2023
